summary: A 1978 survey of ARPANET server hosts, testing how their FTP servers responded when mail was sent to an unknown recipient and when the MLFL command was used instead of MAIL. It reports results of two surveys run in late 1978.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone knocked on many doors with a wrong name and a different kind of letter to see how each computer reacted.

questions: how did early networks transfer mail
why did rfc 751 survey ftp servers
subtitle: A survey of how ARPANET FTP servers handled mail and an alternative mail command

tldr.problem: ARPANET FTP servers had inconsistent behavior for handling mail, especially when sending to unknown recipients or using the MLFL command (an alternative to MAIL that sends mail over a data connection instead of the command connection).
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents two surveys run between September and December 1978. Researchers connected to socket 3 of ARPANET server FTP implementations and tested (1) sending mail to unknown recipients and (2) using the MLFL command instead of the standard MAIL command, then cataloged which servers accepted each, which rejected with errors, and which became unreachable.
tldr.outcome: The results show highly inconsistent behavior across servers: some accepted mail for unknown recipients, others refused, some supported MLFL while others returned unrecognized command errors. This survey exposed the lack of standardization in ARPANET mail handling.

today: RFC 751 is a historical survey documenting the state of ARPANET mail services in 1978. FTP was used for mail transfer on the early Internet, but SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, RFC 821) eventually became the standard. The lack of consensus documented in this RFC motivated work on clearer mail protocols and standards. Today's mail systems benefit from decades of experience solving the consistency problems that RFC 751 exposed.

sections.title: Testing FTP Mail Servers
sections.content:
RFC 751 reports the results of two surveys of ARPANET server hosts conducted between September 20 and December 11, 1978. The surveys tested how FTP servers responded to (1) attempts to send mail to unknown recipients and (2) attempts to use the MLFL command instead of the standard MAIL command.

The goal was to determine which servers accepted mail for unknown users, what error they returned when they refused, and to what extent the MLFL command (which sends mail over a data connection rather than the command connection, avoiding certain end-of-mail and command-reader problems) was supported across the network.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is a report card: the author tried mailing to made-up names at many computers, and separately tried a different kind of mail command, and wrote down what each computer said.

sections.title: MLFL Command Results
sections.content:
The MLFL survey tested 56 server sites by connecting to socket 3 and sending the MLFL command. Seven sites failed to connect or gave anomalous responses (e.g., "INDRA FTP Version 2.00" crashes). Seven sites returned an unrecognized command error (501 or 500 response). Thirty-one sites appeared to support MLFL or proceed through all the right motions, though a few required authentication (USER/PASS) first.

The survey exposed wide variation: most sites that supported MLFL allowed the user to attempt the data connection from their own end, using an RFC queueing algorithm, rather than just listening. Some sites like MIT-MULTICS and RADC-MULTICS required specific credentials before accepting MLFL.
sections.plainLanguage: Of the computers tested, some understood the MLFL command and sent data, some said they did not understand it, and a few just crashed or refused to talk.

sections.title: Mail to Unknown Recipients
sections.content:
The MAIL survey tested how servers responded to sending mail to a fake recipient ("Fzorkness"). Nine sites accepted mail for unknown recipients. Thirty-one sites refused with a 450 error ("No such mailbox") or similar. Seventeen sites returned other errors (user unknown, login required, etc.).

The results show that most servers were protective of their mail systems, refusing to accept messages for nonexistent users. However, a few sites (MIT-AI, MIT-DMS, MIT-MC, BNL, UCLA-CCN, RAND-RCC, and the USC-ISI group) did accept such mail, suggesting different philosophies about forward mail delivery and alias handling.
sections.plainLanguage: Most computers refused to accept mail for people they didn't know. A few accepted it anyway, maybe assuming the mail should be forwarded or queued.

sections.title: What the Survey Shows
sections.content:
The survey reveals that in 1978 there was no consensus on FTP mail behavior. Different hosts made different decisions about accepting or rejecting mail for unknown users, and support for MLFL was spotty. Sites ran different FTP implementations from different vendors (TENEX, Multics, Unix variants, ITS), and each had its own interpretation of how to handle edge cases.

This lack of standardization made it difficult to build reliable mail delivery. The survey data helped the RFC community understand the scope of the problem and motivated later work on standardized SMTP (RFC 821) and other mail protocols that would provide clearer, more consistent semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: The different computers did not agree on basic mail rules. This made it hard to send mail reliably. The survey showed that the network needed clearer standards.
